items.title: 30.4.2 High-Resolution 1H NMR and Splitting of Peaks

source_refs.note: Topic 30.4.2 with Table 30.2 and Quick Check 30.3, as printed (PDF 207-209). The table's peak shapes follow it as the existing drawing.

blocks.text: The NMR signals of protons are not only affected by the nearby electrons, but also by protons on the adjacent atoms. This effect can be observed by a high-resolution NMR. When a high-resolution ¹H NMR spectrum of a molecule is studied, it reveals that each peak is often made up of a cluster of sub-peaks. This is due to the splitting of each signal due to the presence of protons (¹H) on adjacent carbon atoms.

blocks.title: Splitting of signals
blocks.text: The splitting of signals into multiple peaks (e.g., doublets, triplets, quartets) indicates the number of protons (¹H) on the adjacent (neighbouring) carbon atom.
Number of sub-peaks can be calculated by using 'n+1' rule. A signal usually splits into n+1 sub-peaks, where n is the number of protons on adjacent carbon atoms.
(Where n = the number of protons on the adjacent carbon atom).

In the high-resolution ¹H NMR spectrum of ethanol, the -CH₃ peak is split into three sub-peaks (known as triplet) because the number of protons on adjacent carbon is 2 (2+1=3). Similarly, -CH₂- peak is split into four sub-peaks (known as a quartet) because there are 3 protons on its adjacent carbon (3+1=4). The -OH signal is not split because hydrogen is bonded to an oxygen atom instead of carbon atom (Figure 30.5).

blocks.alt: High-resolution spectrum on a scale from 9 to 0 with the formula CH3 - CH2 - OH. A tall single peak labelled 1H at about 5.4, a group of four sub-peaks labelled 2H at about 3.6, and a group of three sub-peaks labelled 3H at about 1.2.
blocks.caption: Figure 30.5: High-resolution 1H NMR spectrum of ethanol (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 30.5).

blocks.text: This is important to note that -OH and -NH protons usually do not show splitting, so these appear as singlet peak. Similarly, chemically equivalent protons do not cause splitting of their neighbouring protons. For example, the ethane (CH₃-CH₃) molecule has two methyl groups attached to each other. If one methyl group is considered, its adjacent carbon has 3 protons attached to it. However, the peak does not show splitting because all the hydrogen atoms in ethane are chemically equivalent (Figure 30.6).

blocks.alt: A spectrum on a scale from 3 to 0 with the formula H3C-CH3 and one sharp, unsplit peak near 0.9.
blocks.caption: Figure 30.6: High-resolution 1H NMR spectrum of ethane (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 30.6).

blocks.text: The number of sub-peaks for different number of neighbouring protons and their appearance given in Table 30.2 is useful to recognise splitting patterns in high-resolution ¹H NMR spectra.

blocks.caption: Table 30.2 Common splitting patterns in high-resolution ¹H NMR spectra
header: No. of Protons on Adjacent Carbon Atom (n)

blocks.alt: The appearance of split peaks from Table 30.2: one peak (singlet, s, n = 0), two equal peaks (doublet, d, n = 1), three peaks with the middle one tallest (triplet, t, n = 2), and four peaks with the inner two tallest (quartet, q, n = 3).

blocks.title: Quick Check 30.3
blocks.text:
a) A signal in the ¹H NMR spectrum is a quartet. How many adjacent, equivalent protons ('n') are there?
b) Calculate the number of sub-peaks for each signal in the high-resolution spectra of the following compounds?
i) butan-2-ol
ii) 1-chloropropane
iii) propanone
iv) 2,2-dimethylpropane
v) methanol
